We ask every candidate the same thing. Ninety days in, what would you bring to this board?
Three recommendations, in order. The first is a quick win: I would recommend that we streamline the monthly close, from nine days to five.
Five days. Is that realistic in an agency group?
It is, if the units send their numbers on day three. So I would insist that every unit head sign off their own figures before they reach finance.
And the second?
The second is about cash. I would suggest that the board ring-fence the technology budget, and that we defer the new office until we know our headroom.
That will not be popular with the creative side.
Probably not. That is why it is essential that the plan be endorsed by the audit committee before it comes to the full board.
And the third?
The third depends on what I find. I would rather put forward a roadmap in month three than promise one today.
Ninety days in, I would bring the board three recommendations, in order.
The third depends on what I find, so I would rather put forward a roadmap in month three.

I chair the board of a media group, and I have interviewed six finance directors in the last ten years. The question I always ask is what they would bring to the board after ninety days. The weak answer is that they would listen. Of course they would listen. The strong answer gives me three things. One problem they expect to find, one quick win they could deliver in the first quarter, and one thing they would deliberately not do yet. The last one is the rarest. A candidate who tells me he would put off a project he likes is a candidate who understands that a board has limited attention, and limited cash.

When I was a young finance director, my board papers were full of soft language. Perhaps we could consider looking at the costs. My chair sent one of them back to me with a single note in the margin: recommend something. So I learned to write it differently. I recommend that the board approve a hiring freeze in the central functions until June. It is essential that the savings be used for the technology project and nothing else. Nobody in that room thought I was being arrogant. They thought I had done the work. A recommendation is a decision you are asking somebody else to take, and it should sound like one.
